video_title: How Britain Abandoned The Working Class | Lisa McKenzie & Keith Gildart
gist: Sociologist Lisa McKenzie and labour historian Keith Gildart argue with Peter McCormack that Britain's post-1980s de-industrialisation was an active policy choice that replaced secure, unionised industrial jobs with a low-wage warehouse-and-services economy sustained by imported labour, welfare top-ups and asset inflation. The practical investor content is political-risk and UK-macro: why de-industrialised constituencies have defected from Labour to Reform, why housing has become the substitute pension, why UK productivity and living standards now trail the US, and which policy shifts (collective bargaining, council-house building, devolution, proportional representation, re-nationalisation of rail and water) the panel expects to gain ground. This is a sociological/historical episode with no tickers or trade calls.

insights.claim: Keith Gildart frames the collapse of Britain's working-class world as deliberate policy rather than market drift, dating it from the mid-1970s and locating the active dismantling in the 1980s-90s under both Conservative and New Labour governments.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: If regional decline is read as a policy artefact rather than an accident, the political demand for policy reversal (industrial subsidy, re-nationalisation, labour re-regulation) is structurally durable, not a passing populist mood.
insights.quote: there was active policies that dismantled the working class

insights.claim: UK coal employment fell from over a million at the outbreak of WWI to roughly 15,000 miners by the early 1990s, with the last mine closing in 2015 — a labour-market contraction whose pace, not just scale, destroyed the communities built around it.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the speed at which a single-industry regional economy can be liquidated; a useful base rate when modelling energy-transition or AI-driven displacement in concentrated labour markets.
insights.quote: And then you get to a point in the early 1990s where there's around 15,000 miners left. Then we move forward to 2015, the last mine closes.

insights.claim: Gildart notes that former coal-mine sites are now typically occupied by Amazon warehouses and out-of-town retail, so the same land base now supports far lower-paid, lower-security employment than the industry it replaced.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: The physical substitution of logistics for extraction is the clearest map of where UK regional wage compression happened — relevant to warehouse-labour cost, unionisation risk and local political sentiment around distribution assets.
insights.quote: if you go to places where there were former coal mines cuz often you find there now Amazon warehouses,

insights.claim: Lisa McKenzie dates the second shock in Nottinghamshire to Marks and Spencer's 1990 decision to abandon made-in-England sourcing for competitiveness, which closed the textile factories employing women at the same moment the pits closed and removed both male and female employment simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A concrete case that single-retailer sourcing decisions can be the proximate trigger for regional collapse — supply-chain reshoring debates carry the same leverage in reverse.
insights.quote: 1990 Marks and Spencers changes its policy and they say right we need to be more competitive.

insights.claim: In Shirebrook, the closed pit site was replaced by a Sports Direct warehouse roughly four miles square that recruited directly from Poland, creating a decade of local ethnic friction before the two working-class groups integrated around a revived market.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Illustrates the recruit-abroad model that anchored UK warehouse wage floors, and the local social-licence risk that follows large single-employer distribution sites.

insights.claim: McKenzie reports that automation has cut the same Sports Direct-style warehouse headcount from roughly 200 to around 50, and that Polish workers are now returning home — meaning the replacement employer is itself now shedding the jobs it created.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Warehouse automation is already producing a second round of regional job loss and net outward migration of workers — a leading indicator for both local demand and further political radicalisation in those seats.
insights.quote: A lot of the Polish are actually going home. They're going back.

insights.claim: The panel argues the loss from pit closures was social infrastructure, not only wages: with mass unemployment the butchers, sandwich shops, pubs and miners' welfares died too, councils used the empty model villages to house difficult tenants, and crime, ill health and addiction followed.
insights.speaker: guest, academic
insights.so_what: A template for second-order local-economy collapse: anchor-employer loss propagates through retail, housing quality and public-health costs, which is where fiscal cost eventually lands.
insights.quote: it's it's a disintegration of the social fabric

themes.theme: Low-Wage Equilibrium and Immigration as Labour Supply

insights.claim: McKenzie's critique of recent immigration is economic rather than racial: bringing people in specifically for the lowest-paid jobs has, in her view, stabilised low pay by creating a permanent oversupply of workers willing to accept the bottom rate.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: If the political consensus shifts to treating migration as a wage-suppression mechanism rather than a race question, labour-intensive sectors (hospitality, care, logistics, agriculture) face a structural cost shock.
insights.quote: So what that has done it has stabilized low pay.

insights.claim: The panel contrasts post-war migration, which fed defined labour demand in brickworks, transport, engineering and the mines and assimilated arrivals directly into the working class, with the last decade's migration, which they say has had no coherent economic story attached to it.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Frames the political fault line as demand-led versus supply-led migration — the distinction that any workable UK visa reform will have to be sold on.

insights.claim: Gildart argues the right's position is internally contradictory: the same politicians campaigning to be tough on immigration built and defended the low-pay economy that generates the demand for imported labour.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Implies migration cuts without wage-floor and productivity reform will not stick, keeping policy volatility high for labour-dependent business models.
insights.quote: It's the economy that they've supported has led to this right of low pay economy.

insights.claim: McCormack attributes the cheap-labour settlement to corporate lobbying rather than middle-class consumer preference, citing hotel chains and London restaurants where the workforce he observes is now overwhelmingly foreign-born.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Locates the political target as employer lobbying, which is where restriction, if it comes, would bite margins first — hospitality and hotel operators.
insights.quote: And there's been a significant amount of lobbying to allow that to happen to keep the wages down at the highest level.

insights.claim: Both academics argue the state is now effectively subsidising employers and landlords, because wages are too low to live on and the benefit system tops them up — an outcome they call absurd given the right's stated opposition to state intervention.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Framing in-work benefits as an employer subsidy is the intellectual groundwork for wage-floor increases or employer levies; watch it migrate into mainstream party platforms.
insights.quote: as taxpayers we're subsidizing employers because their wages are so low

insights.claim: McKenzie says private renters at the bottom of the market are paying around 60% of earnings in rent and using food banks in order to service it, and cites a nurse at a Bedford-area food bank saying she does not earn enough to get by.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A rent-to-income ratio at that level in the bottom quartile caps discretionary consumer spending and raises the political probability of rent controls or aggressive social-housing build.
insights.quote: it's costing them 60% of their earnings

themes.theme: Class as Capital: Networks, Education and the Access Filter

insights.claim: McKenzie's core claim is that social mobility in Britain has stopped, so birth position now predicts destination — a position she concedes meritocrats reject but says the data supports.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A frozen mobility regime is a slow-burn political-risk input: it sustains anti-incumbent voting regardless of which party holds office.
insights.quote: social mobility in this country has stopped

insights.claim: McKenzie uses Bourdieu's four capitals — economic, social, cultural and symbolic — as her working model of class, arguing outcomes are set by the interaction between them rather than income alone, which is why a six-figure plumber and a £40k graduate sit differently in the structure.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A more predictive segmentation of UK consumers and voters than income deciles — useful for reading which cohorts actually convert income into assets.

insights.claim: Only 7% of UK children are privately educated but that group dominates the professions, journalism, politics and the culture industries, which McKenzie calls 'interesting work' — access to which now requires being in London and able to work unpaid.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Unpaid-internship dependence concentrates media and policy narrative-setting in one funded cohort — a structural reason UK public discourse under-prices regional grievance.
insights.quote: and also that 7% then dominate the professions

insights.claim: McKenzie cites a December conference finding that only 5% of people working in television are working class, arguing the national story is therefore told through a single class lens and this is the root of political alienation.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Media composition is a leading indicator of polling error: narrative producers systematically miss the electorate that decides marginal seats.
insights.quote: only 5% of the people who work in television are working class

insights.claim: McKenzie declines to attack private education directly, arguing it is a better product that legitimately buys advantage and networks, and that reformers should instead fix state provision — she and Gildart also reject the framing that the problem is a lack of working-class ambition.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A left-of-centre voice declining to back abolition narrows the realistic policy space on private education, and shifts it toward state-school funding fights.
insights.quote: You're buying a decent education, but you're also buying a network as well.

insights.claim: Gildart says strong regional accents measurably reduce entry into elite professions, citing academic hiring panels where candidates were rated as sounding less intelligent, and both guests argue class should become a protected characteristic.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: A campaign to add class to protected characteristics would create new UK employer compliance and reporting obligations — an under-watched regulatory tail risk.
insights.quote: we think class should be a protected characteristic

insights.claim: McKenzie argues Britain's monitoring framework hides white working-class outcomes because there is only one white box on ethnicity forms, so white council-estate children are counted alongside Eton pupils, and she says both boys and now girls in that group sit at the bottom on education, health and jobs.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A measurement gap of this kind is where policy failures accumulate unpriced; it also explains why the grievance surfaces politically before it surfaces in official data.
insights.quote: But there's only one white box.

insights.claim: McKenzie links entrenched class bigotry — the Vicky Pollard caricature and the early sexualisation of white working-class girls — to Britain's slowness in confronting the grooming-gangs scandal, arguing the prejudice suppressed scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Explains the intensity of the issue in exactly the de-industrialised seats now swinging to Reform — a driver of local political volatility that national polling narratives tend to miss.

themes.theme: Political Realignment: Labour's Collapse, Reform and Devolution

insights.claim: McKenzie notes Labour has replaced the language of class with the phrase 'working people' precisely to avoid class analysis, and both guests read Andy Burnham's recent reversion to 'working-class people' as a deliberate signal.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Language shifts precede platform shifts; a Labour move back to explicit class framing would presage redistribution and labour-market policy, not just rhetoric.

insights.claim: Gildart traces Labour's loss of the de-industrialised seats to the Mandelson assumption that those voters had nowhere else to go, an assumption disproved once the working class lost its economic and political weight.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: The captured-vote model is broken across Western social-democratic parties; expect continued fragmentation and coalition instability in UK electoral pricing.
insights.quote: Well, they'll always vote Labor anyway. These people will always vote Labor.

insights.claim: McKenzie dates Labour's decline in mining seats to 1997 onward and blames parachuting cabinet figures into safe seats — Mandelson in Hartlepool, Tristram Hunt in Stoke-on-Trent — as the visible proof to voters that the party was not theirs.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Candidate-selection centralisation is a measurable, forward-looking predictor of incumbent-party defection in specific constituencies.

insights.claim: McKenzie argues working-class voters moved to Reform not out of ideology but because they know their communities were abandoned, tried Brexit and Boris Johnson in 2019 as change votes, and reached for the next available disruption — a small-r rebellion.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: If the driver is serial change-seeking rather than party loyalty, Reform's own vote is unstable too — sequential protest realignment, not a durable new bloc.

insights.claim: McKenzie defends Reform's net effect on British politics as disruptive and useful while explicitly saying Nigel Farage would be a terrible prime minister and that the party has frightened the establishment.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Separates disruption value from governing capability — the same distinction markets should apply when pricing a Reform-influenced parliament versus a Reform-led one.
insights.quote: the reason why they've been good for British politics is because they've disrupted it

insights.claim: Gildart counters that Reform are essentially Thatcherite rightists whose non-immigration policies would do nothing for de-industrialised communities, pointing to their vote against the extension of workers' rights, and argues the rise of the right historically pulls Labour rightward rather than energising the left.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Implies a Reform-pressured parliament produces tighter immigration plus continued deregulation — a policy mix that keeps labour costs low but does not resolve regional grievance.
insights.quote: They voted against the extension to workers rights.

insights.claim: Gildart cites Burnham winning the 97%-white former Reform-leaning Makerfield constituency, and reports meeting three pub regulars who vote Reform in general elections but Burnham for Manchester Mayor — evidence that ticket-splitting by office is now normal in these seats.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Mayoral incumbents can hold ground national parties are losing; devolved city-region politics is where UK policy experimentation and infrastructure money will concentrate.
insights.quote: they vote reform in a general election in the last election but they vote Burnham for Manchester Mayor

insights.claim: Gildart flags the rise of English nationalism as the under-discussed parallel to the SNP and Plaid Cymru capturing de-industrialised working-class votes in Scotland and Wales, moving from fringe to mainstream party language.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: A four-nations fragmentation of the working-class vote raises the odds of constitutional questions returning to the UK policy agenda.

insights.claim: Gildart's structural fixes are proportional representation and genuine devolution, arguing the Labour landslide was a landslide in seats but not in votes and that centralisation since the 1980s stripped councils of power and disconnected voters.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Seats-versus-votes divergence is the mechanism that makes UK majorities brittle; electoral-reform pressure is a live medium-term political risk.
insights.quote: we got to have proportional representation for a start

insights.claim: Both guests and the host converge on a political-class critique: Britain moved from electing miners and steelworkers to a graduate professional class, and McKenzie is pessimistic because she does not believe current politicians even understand the problem — neither guest could name a politician they like other than Burnham.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Low confidence in the political class among sympathetic experts argues for continued policy incoherence and elevated UK political-risk premia.
insights.quote: we used to be electing miners, steel workers, you know, up to the 1980s. It's a graduate class.

insights.claim: McKenzie argues New Labour's redistribution was never structural — tax credits and community grants sloshed money around without changing the system — so when the 2008 crash and 2010 austerity removed the money, the gains vanished instantly.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A template for evaluating any transfer-based programme: cash top-ups without structural change are pro-cyclical and evaporate at exactly the wrong point in the cycle.
insights.quote: All they'd done is sloshed money around.

insights.claim: McKenzie says Blairism expanded the state by creating large numbers of low-paid public-sector jobs — teaching assistants, city security — so the same people de-industrialised in the 1980s were made redundant a second time when austerity hit.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Public-sector job creation as a substitute for a productive base leaves regional employment directly geared to the fiscal cycle — a repeatable vulnerability.
insights.quote: The minute the money wasn't there, all those jobs disappeared overnight.

insights.claim: McKenzie argues the housing market was destroyed by turning the home into a required investment: thirty years ago a house was where you lived, now it has to function as the pension.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Explains the political impossibility of falling house prices in the UK: homeowners are pension-holders, so supply reform is structurally blocked from below as well as above.
insights.quote: 30 years ago your house wasn't an investment. It was it was where you lived. Now it has to be your pension

insights.claim: Working-class redundancy money from industrial closures was often converted into a second property to rent out, deliberately used as a private pension substitute after occupational pensions and bank savings rates were destroyed.
insights.speaker: guest, academic
insights.so_what: A large slice of the UK small-landlord base is retirement provision, not speculation — which is why buy-to-let tax changes hit a politically sensitive, non-wealthy constituency.

insights.claim: McCormack's monetary thesis is that expanding the money supply distributes unevenly — those with credit access take loans in a depreciating currency and buy appreciating assets — so both working and middle classes get destroyed unless the money system is fixed.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: The Cantillon-effect framing is the host's core lens; it maps inequality debates onto long-asset, short-cash positioning rather than onto tax policy.
insights.quote: They they they take a loan in the depreciating currency and they buy the appreciated assets.

insights.claim: McCormack states the UK now spends more on debt interest alone than on education, and argues government debt plus money printing is the upstream cause of stagnant wages and falling living standards.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Frames UK gilt-market constraints as the binding limit on any redistribution programme the panel proposes — the fiscal ceiling on all the policy asks in this episode.
insights.quote: We spend more now on debt in just interest than we spend on education.

insights.claim: McKenzie accepts the monetary argument to the extent that post-2008 money creation did not circulate as promised but accumulated at the top, with the 0.1% getting steadily richer while those at the bottom got poorer.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Notable convergence: a left sociologist and a Bitcoin host agree QE was the distributional turning point — a cross-ideological consensus that makes monetary-reform politics more likely, not less.
insights.quote: And what we saw after 2008 is that 0.1% of society get richer and richer and richer.

insights.claim: McKenzie treats the ubiquity of passive-income advice as diagnostic evidence that labour no longer pays, and the panel agrees that the ultimate test of the system is whether work funds a house, a holiday and a car.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: A simple, testable political threshold: while wages fail that test, redistribution and anti-asset-owner politics keep gaining regardless of party.
insights.quote: that's an admittance that your labor your work isn't paying

insights.claim: McCormack argues inequality itself is not the problem provided productivity rises and everyone's standards improve, and both guests accept the framing that the real failure is falling living standards for everyone outside the top.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Reframes UK politics as a productivity problem rather than a distribution problem — the version of the argument most likely to survive across the political divide.

themes.theme: Unions, Workers' Rights and the Cost of Employing

insights.claim: McKenzie's policy priority for a serious Labour party is workplace rights that enable wage campaigning, collective bargaining agreements and stronger trade union rights, ahead of transfer payments.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Sectoral bargaining is the most plausible UK labour-cost shock over the next parliament; it would hit low-margin, labour-heavy sectors first.
insights.quote: I'd have collective bargaining agreements, more rights for trade unions.

insights.claim: Gildart wants full repeal of the Conservative-era anti-trade-union laws, arguing that historically working-class living standards only improved through self-organisation in the workplace and community.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: A concrete, costable legislative ask — repeal would raise UK strike risk and bargaining power in transport, logistics and public services.
insights.quote: I want the repeal of all the anti-trade union laws that were introduced by the Conservatives.

insights.claim: McCormack reports that in his own coffee shop half of revenue goes on wages and about 25% on taxes and regulation, leaving no profit, and says day-one employment rights make him actively disinclined to start businesses because a single disruptive hire can cost tens of thousands in a two-year process.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: A first-hand unit-economics read on UK hospitality: wage plus regulatory load at that ratio implies continued closures and hiring freezes in small-scale services.
insights.quote: Half my money goes on wages and about 25% goes on taxes and regulations. We don't make any money.

insights.claim: McCormack distinguishes workplace-level unionisation, which he supports, from national unions trading political endorsements for policy — arguing the latter reproduces the corporate lobbying he objects to.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Enterprise bargaining versus national bargaining is the fault line to watch in any UK labour reform; the two have very different cost profiles for employers.

insights.claim: McKenzie argues legislation like the Greens' proposed maximum workplace temperature is only necessary because shop stewards no longer exist on site — her mother settled heat breaks at the tights factory informally, whereas today's paid union officials trigger formal legal process.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Explains the ratchet from workplace relations to litigation: as on-site representation disappeared, compliance cost migrated into statute and lawyers — a one-way cost trend for employers.
insights.quote: And that isn't trade union power gone mad, is it?

themes.theme: Britain's Decline versus the US: Productivity, Emigration and Social Fabric

insights.claim: McCormack cites the survey ranking the UK below Mississippi if it were a US state, notes British people guess it would rank around seventh, and says US productivity and GDP growth are rising while the UK's are stagnant.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: The relative-income gap is now the argument driving UK skilled emigration and capital allocation abroad — a compounding drag on UK domestic assets.
insights.quote: The bottom poorer than Mississippi.

insights.claim: Gildart argues the middle class holds an exit option the working class does not — the ability to simply leave the country for Australia or America — which he considers the grossly unfair part of the current settlement.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Elite exit removes exactly the taxpayers and reformers a recovery would need; watch UK skilled-emigration data as a leading indicator of fiscal deterioration.
insights.quote: If if you're from the middle class, you've got another benefit that maybe working class have. You can just leave the country.

insights.claim: In Gildart's research on Leigh in Greater Manchester, young people who leave for university in Manchester do not return, so de-industrialised constituencies are left with a distinctive older, non-graduate demographic that correlates with Reform strength.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Internal brain drain hard-codes the political geography: these seats will keep voting anti-incumbent because the mobile cohort has already left.
insights.quote: when the young people leave there to go to university, if they go to Manchester, they don't go back

insights.claim: The panel argues middle-class precarity is now spreading — salaries in the lower tiers of accountancy, law and architecture have dropped, young middle-class people cannot get on the housing ladder, and Gildart asks what the Conservatives will have left to conserve.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Professional-services wage compression plus housing exclusion moves a traditionally conservative cohort into the change-voting bloc — the biggest single swing factor in UK politics.

insights.claim: McCormack raises the question, from his earlier David Goodhart interview, of whether AI will do to the graduate elite what factory closures did to industrial workers, and believes they are about to experience it.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: If AI displacement lands on graduate professions, the political coalition for labour protection widens dramatically — a scenario with direct implications for regulation of AI deployment.

insights.claim: Gildart notes a genuine cross-party shift in that both right and left now concede rail privatisation and the water companies were failures, which he treats as the first real acknowledgement that the 1980s model did not deliver.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Cross-party consensus against privatisation is the precondition for further re-nationalisation — a direct regulatory and ownership risk for UK regulated utilities and rail operators.
insights.quote: even people on the right or the left for example say the railways have been a disaster

insights.claim: Asked who Britain is for now, the answer given is the people who profited from the 1980s and 1990s changes — landlords owning dozens of houses, speculators and consultancy companies taking large government contracts — with McKenzie adding that the only way to get rich now is taking government money.
insights.speaker: guest, academic
insights.so_what: Rent-extraction from the state as the perceived route to wealth is the political case for procurement and landlord crackdowns — the two most exposed UK cash-flow streams if sentiment converts into policy.
insights.quote: The only way you can get rich now is taking government money.

insights.claim: Neither guest nor host could name a single government-provided service that has improved in the last twenty years, with education, health, borders and roads all cited as worse — McKenzie's only positive was mass university access, which she says was ruined by the loan system.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: A blunt state-capacity read from across the political spectrum: assume continued public-service underperformance when modelling UK fiscal outcomes and political churn.
insights.quote: It's a debt trap actually.

insights.claim: The panel argues Britain's decline narrative is now qualitatively different from the 1960s-70s version because it is driven by genuine fear and precarity, alongside erosion of the social fabric — boarded-up pubs made unaffordable to run, dead Labour, Conservative and Liberal clubs, and politics relocated from communities to Westminster.
insights.speaker: Keith Gildart
insights.so_what: Loss of physical civic infrastructure removes the mechanism that historically absorbed political anger locally — a structural argument for higher volatility in UK politics.
insights.quote: there's a genuine fear in society now people are genuinely frightened

insights.claim: McKenzie says the recovery story has to be local voice and local power, arguing every area would rise if it could act for itself, but that this is impossible under a centralised government constantly bashing local authorities.
insights.speaker: Lisa McKenzie
insights.so_what: Aligns with Gildart's devolution case and with Burnham's mayoral model — the concrete direction UK regional policy is drifting, and where local infrastructure spend is likely to be directed.

insights.claim: Both academics report that UK research funding bodies will not fund work on de-industrialisation and working-class communities, with multiple rejected bids including one on Bedford and Luton after the car industry losses.
insights.speaker: guest, academic
insights.so_what: A data gap by design: the empirical base for the fastest-moving UK political trend is systematically underfunded, which is why forecasters keep being surprised by these constituencies.
insights.quote: The world of academia are not interested in those things.
